utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, before we pick up your account from what happened once you got to Dubravica, I want a little more detail in relation to events that occurred while you were waiting in the stream or ditch, and in particular I want your help, if you can provide it, with identities of any of the soldiers that you saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've told Mr. Stein what I have in mind to do, and I think that largely it will be non-contentious and therefore it may be possible to lead with names. Mr. Stein will tell if and when he wants things dealt with otherwise. The names are dealt with, for Mr. Stein's assistance and Mr. Kovacic's, in the statement of the 3rd of February, '95, and the additional document of the 1st of February, '97. I'm on page 4 of the first statement, towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The two men who came to your house and killed your father and brother, did any of them look familiar to you and appear as somebody you had seen in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The younger one looked familiar to me, and I think I used to meet him in the Leptir Discotheque near Busovaca. My guess is he comes from the village of Buselji or below Buselji, another village called Bare.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know he was a member of an armed group before you saw him at your house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A matter of detail from when you were in the stream or ditch. Did you actually see something of the destruction of the mosque in Ahmici, in that you saw, I think, people go to the mosque, entering it, and subsequently you saw the top of the minaret blown off?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was the period of the 20th of October, when I saw the top of the minaret gone. And also on the 17th of April, '93, I also saw the minaret go off, so that it was on two occasions that I witnessed the demolition of minarets. On two occasions, therefore, in October '92 and April '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with the April '93 damage and destruction, had you seen anything of people entering and leaving the mosque before and after the damage or did you just see the damage from a distance?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I spotted a car arriving from the direction of Busovaca, and from it emerged military policemen who moved towards the mosque, and a terrific explosion could be heard immediately afterwards. Right after the explosion, the same car came near me where I was hiding, to the house in which I was hiding, and those were military policemen from Busovaca and their commander; that is, I concluded that from the talk amongst them which I overheard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you hear them say?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, first the way in which they greeted one another, and the two of them who one of them asked, "What's new in Busovaca?" "Everything is all right. And what about you?" And he would say, "Commander, we've got a Mujahedin here captured. What are we to do with him?" Then the commander says, "Well, throw a bomb, kill him."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with soldiers you saw while you were in the ditch, was one of them known to you by the nickname Cico or similar? This is page 5 of the first document and, I think, amplified or corrected in the second document at page 7. The name Cico?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is a nickname, Cico, but his name was Nikica Safradin and he was the first one to bring those soldiers. He seemed to be sort of a commander of the military police, and I saw that he was the one who deployed or rather tasked those soldiers. I also recognised Dragan Santic. Dragan Santic comes from Rovna, and Ilija Santic, whom I also saw there, came from the village of Mahala. I also saw Dragan Matkovic's brother who attended the same class with me in school, and one of Jozo Matkovic's son from the village of Rijeka. Also Blaz Totic. He wore civilian clothes, and he used to be the driver at the company called Masinogradnja, where I was employed once. Those were, by and large, men I recognised and knew their names. I also knew some people from Vitez. That is, I knew them by sight, but I don't know their names. There were quite a number of them who came from around Vitez, I mean in that group which arrived together with Safradin. I even noticed some men who had their heads masked, that is, they had black socks over their heads, and some in civilian clothes but carrying arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The named men, did you know any, some, or all of them to be members of a military unit before the time that you saw them from your vantage point in the ditch?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew about Cico. I knew he was a member of the military police. Santic, Ilija Santic, he also was with the military police before that attack, because I used to see both of them at checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A matter of detail. When the grenade or bomb was thrown into the house in which you were hiding after you had spent the day in the ditch, did you see what sort of device it was, how it was supposed to cause damage?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a so-called Kasikara, a grenade which was thrown at me. It was black.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a result of the explosion, did you lose substantial hearing in your left ear?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did, yes, my hearing was damaged, I believe around 80 per cent in my left ear, and I keep hearing a buzzing sound ever since that explosion, to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When the two Croats to whom you turned for help took you away, did you learn of the death of your -- no, I beg your pardon, did you ask them to deal with the burial of your father and brother and say they could take 400 Deutschmarks from your father's pocket to bury them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And again, I'm going to deal with this by leading, unless it's not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In fact, did you understand there were other people dealing specifically with the burial of the dead, but you subsequently were informed that your father's body had been reburied in order that somebody could take the 400 D-marks out of his pocket? If that's correct, please just say "yes".

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It was done by a young man called Dalibor. He was one who did it. But I learned that later, after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Answer "Yes" or "No," please, to the next question or series of questions, when it's possible: Did you subsequently hear from other people about units who may have been involved in the massacre or the attack on this day?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard that units which were called Jokers --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The answer is supposed to be yes --

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, I think, is content.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm content with the answer, but as to the next question, I think you ought to let him answer on his own as opposed to telling him the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us who it was, then, you heard about, and from whom you heard it.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear about a group said to be involved, and if so, from whom did you hear about this group?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard it later, after the conflict. That is when I heard about that name -- that is, Jokers, Jokeri -- and that they took part, and that also there were others, called Vitezovi, who committed those butcheries. But it was only after I had arrived in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And who told you, if you can remember, about those groups and their involvement?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't really recall just now, but people talked about it. It was common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Secondly, was there any reference to people coming from Croatia itself?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed, I heard also about those men in black uniforms and that they came from Varazdin. I heard that from Ferid Ahmic, also after the conflict. For a while, he was even a member of HOS, and on the eve of the attack on the 16th of April, he lived in the village of Nadioci, so that he did have some more information, and he told me that men in black uniforms came from as far as Varazdin -- rather, were brought from as far as Varazdin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Varazdin is in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in which direction from Ahmici? Towards the coast?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Varazdin is rather far away. It is close to the Slovenian border, so to the west of Ahmici, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we pick the account you gave yesterday up at your journey to Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To remind the judges of the geography, if they need it, it might be helpful for the maps to go back on the ELMO, starting with the overhead map, with Number 1.980 on top of that, which we looked at, but very briefly, yesterday, and with the smaller maps available, please. If you're looking at that map, you were taken in a column -- and you are looking at map 1.980 -- you were taken in a column to Dubravica school?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At Dubravica, were men segregated from women?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were, but not all of them, because there was no room for women in the place where they were trying to put them up, so there were also some in the gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many people were there altogether, so far as you could judge?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The largest number was -- they were brought in group after group. I should say, when I came there, that there were about 500 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just "Yes" or "No," please, to this question: Did you hear something of what may have happened to some women? Just "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From whom did you hear what may have happened to some women?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard that directly from a woman who had told her husband, and he was right next to me, he was lying on the same mat with me, so that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Therefore, can you please tell us what you heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, I would have to object. This is as to crimes, and, of course, by its very nature, is testimony about crime, from a victim who is telling her husband, apparently, who is then telling this witness. The prejudicial of this is clearly outweighed by the level of hearsay. We're essentially getting into testimony about acts from another person to another person to this person. It's one thing to have hearsay levels on background or corroborative evidence, but this goes directly to the corpus of a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It makes no difference that the evidence is about a crime. What does make a difference is as to whether it is potentially reliable or not. As far as that's concerned, each case will be or may be different; it will depend on the circumstances. We are prepared to admit this evidence, for what it's worth, and we'll have to decide whether it's worth anything or not. Let me just say this to the witness: Mr. Ahmic, we are making some rulings about evidence. It's no reflection on you or the evidence; it's to do with the Rules of Evidence in the Tribunal. So if I have appeared to make some sort of comment about it, don't take any notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what you heard about the treatment of women?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I may, could I just go back to what the gentleman said, that it was hearsay: It wasn't. It was direct knowledge, because I heard it from the woman herself, so that it is not second-hand information. It is first-hand information. She was about a metre a away from me. I cannot give you the names of other women who were raped; I learned about those later, and that indeed is hearsay. But I know of at least two more women who had been raped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom did they say they'd been raped, if they identified perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, I did not hear that, but those were -- those could be Croat soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From the date of your arrival at the camp, were people taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many per day or night, roughly, if you can help?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were being taken out in groups of ten, all the time, to different areas around Vitez: To Krcevine, to Pirici, Rijeka, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Voluntarily, or by compulsion?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the outset, they would ask if there were any volunteers, and then at a later stage, they took them by compulsion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the camp, did some of the soldiers there have ribbons on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I only spotted one soldier with a blue ribbon like the one worn by those two who shot at me. I noticed that one of the soldiers had that ribbon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What rank did he have in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think he was the deputy of the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness please have, now, for -- no, I'll finish this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You stayed at the camp for, I think, five days before the Red Cross came and registered you. You were checked one day by a doctor, a CBS film crew came and visited you, and in due course, you were moved from Dubravica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: (No microphone)

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you haven't been able to return to live in your own home, and you haven't been back to Ahmici save to visit it, to see -- for whatever reason -- since?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was impossible, because the line had already been positioned, and the war between Bosnians and Croats was in full swing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness please have the Plan 1.593,1, and the Chamber will find the irregular white shape takes -- again, it has to be viewed upside down -- takes you to the road above the mosque at Ahmici and shows in a little more detail what lies to the north and east of that part of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just help us swiftly, if you can, with the points marked here. The numbers and the letters are upside down. What houses are these of significance, please? Use the pointer, and just tell us. 55?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: 55 is Sukrija Ahmici's house. "K," the letter "K," is Vlatko Kupreskic's storage space, storage facility. "C" is--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nice, what's the relevance -- I'm sorry, Mr. Ahmic, to interrupt, but what's the relevant of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to deal with the photographs which come next, and very quickly, which show the level of destruction of Muslim properties and the non-destruction of non-Muslim properties, and I'm just fitting them into the geography to assist the Court, and it won't take very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other houses, "K," "C," and "J," -- well, you've dealt with "K"; "C" and "J" are what?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "C" is Zoran Kupreskic's house, "J" is his uncle's house, and this one here is Miro Kupreskic's and Miro Kupreskic's father's house. His father's name was Ante.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now please take the first of two albums of photographs, which we can deal with very swiftly, because they've got indices at their front. This one is Exhibit 1.593A. Your Honour, the witness has been through these photographs. The index may stand effectively as his evidence in chief, if that's acceptable to the Tribunal in the interests of speed. One can move swiftly through the photographs to see houses that are destroyed, pausing at photograph 4 to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may just be helpful to go through them, since we --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The photographs, then, should go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, just simply go through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Photograph 1, photograph 2, photograph 3 show destroyed houses in Ahmici of Fatima Patkovic, Esad Ahmici and probably of Husein Ahmici. Photograph 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 show the mosque at Gornji Ahmici. Photograph 9 shows the house or the houses of Nermin Kermo and Nesim Ahmic, both destroyed. Photograph 10, Midhat Berbic. Photograph 11, Jahija Pezer in Grabovi, part of Ahmici. 12, the house of Sukrija Ahmic. 13 I don't think we need trouble with. 14 is the undamaged house of Vlatko Kupreskic, and we've seen the general location. 15, the house of Hazim Ahmic, with writing on it to the general effect, "Every Turk who comes back will be slaughtered."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Just for the record, I don't object to this proceeding or process, but it's important, as to this photo which is at 15 and the other photos which have markings on the walls and graffiti, to use our expression, to note that this witness has not been back to Ahmici since the 16th of April, 1993, and we have no idea when these various graffiti or markings with pens were placed, but presumptively after the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will find out when the photographs were taken in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In due course. I think the witness has been back, but not to stay. 17, the school. 18, the house of Hazim Ahmic. 19, the mosque with the minaret lying horizontal. 20, the mosque at Donji Ahmici, and 21 -- I beg your pardon. 22, the graffiti. I accept entirely Mr. Stein's point about the likely dating of the graffiti. Of course, it's after the event. "Goodbye, balijas." 23, a larger photograph with writing on the wall referring to "Disco, 48 hours of ashes," working from 16th of April, '93. 24, the house of Abdulah Ahmic. 25, Sefer Ahmic's house. 26, the mosque again with the words "Croatia". 27, the house on the left, Nedzib Ahmic; the house on the right, Zijad Ahmic. Then 28, Husein Ahmic, is a house. 29, Biat Bilic's house. 30, Fehim Ahmic. 31 -- I beg your pardon. 30 was Hilmija Ahmic. 31, Fehim Ahmic. 32, Sidija Ahmic's house. 33, Redzo Pezer, "Merry Christmas balijas. Welcome," in a church or village, "Welcome. It will be the same." 34, "Only 117 casualties" written on this house. "The country ready. Dangerous for life. Attention, please." 35, the house of Sakir Ahmici. 36, we needn't trouble with. The second smaller black-and-white --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Excuse me for a second. I don't object to the admissibility, and because of the professional nature of the Court, I only rise to once again point out that the prejudicial language not linked to our clients, graffiti after the fact, has been admitted, and we ask the Court essentially to ignore it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The smaller album of black-and-white photographs that I ask the witness to have has got individual numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They were made available on the desk yesterday. They have been distributed to the Defence. I'm so sorry, I thought they had been. They contain, materially, the undamaged minaret, the undamaged houses, and one or two family photographs that the witness has provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What exhibit number is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They've got individual exhibit numbers on the index rather than a collective number, and the numbers are shown as 1531, 1749, and so on. If it would be more convenient for this exhibit to be allocated a comprehensive number, I'll organise that maybe at the break and notify the Court of it. It probably would be more convenient to deal with it that way. Indeed, I imagine the most sensible thing for it to be would be to be 1593B, if that would be convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I pass quickly, because I think this will help, to the second photograph. The first one has got graffiti. The second one is the minaret, undamaged. The third photograph is damaged after the attack on the 28th of October, with damage at the top. It's not, I'm afraid, very clear, but we've at least heard about it. Then the next photograph is the house of Dragan and Ivo Papic, of whom we've heard, Croats. Then the next photograph is the undamaged shop of the Kupreskics' or the warehouse. The following photograph of two undamaged houses is the undamaged houses of Ivica Kupreskic's house and Zoran's house, Zoran Kupreskic's house. The following photograph is the undamaged house of Mirjan, father of Ante Kupreskic. I will ask the witness if he can just look at the following photograph, 1532,3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that house, please, or any house here?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the house of the butcher (indicating) who we used to call Zilo. There is a butcher shop here (indicating), and the third house behind it is where I was brought, along with some women later when they took us to Dubravica, the third house when you go this way here (indicating). This is the main Vitez-Busovaca road (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There follows photographs of your late brother, your late mother as a younger woman. That's your brother and your late mother as a younger woman, and other family members in the last photograph. You haven't yet told us, but the position is that your mother and sister who were left at the house, they were killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just leave that last photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. They were killed in the upper village of Ahmici, my mother and all three sisters. I concluded this from the statement made by Bob Stewart, the commander of the British Battalion, when CNN reports showed the house, and he said that a woman and her daughters had been killed there. Since I knew that in Ahmici there were no other women with more than one daughter who might have been killed, I knew that it was them, and it's the house of Dzemal Ahmic and his son Husein. I concluded this from the report, and I saw the house in the exhibits shown just a short while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This photograph has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in any event, he hasn't seen them since that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But this photograph shows whom, please, Mr. Ahmic, the photograph we're now looking at?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is my youngest sister Alma (indicating). This is my cousin Samir (indicating), who was also killed in the attack on the 16th of April. This is another relative of mine (indicating), and these two children (indicating) are not related to me. This was taken at a birthday party in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Finally by way of the map, and I'm not going to ask you to deal with it in any detail because you've dealt with it on an earlier occasion and it's available for questioning, if asked, may he just see, please, 1979? Again if we have the large-scale map open first to remind the Tribunal -- yes, the large-scale map, this one. No, you were right the first time. Lay that out. Thank you. That's right. Thank you very much. If you now put the other map on top of it, and again upside down, please, and we can see how one relates to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This shows, Mr. Ahmic, does it not, the area between Ahmici and Santici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This is the hamlet of Zume, which belongs to Santici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A number of houses have been marked, and are you in a position to deal, if asked, with either many or all of those houses and who lived in them at the time? I'm not going to ask you, but if asked, if anybody else wants to know, you can deal with the detail of many of these houses?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question is this: Mr. Stein may care to look at page 8 of the statement of the 3rd of February. There were different commanders in charge of the different localities, Nadioci and so on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my statements, I mentioned the local commanders from Nadioci to Santici. If you want, I can state their names again, who they were, in my opinion. I know that in Nadioci, it was Branko. His name was Branko. I can't recall his last name. Oh, Perkovic, Branko Perkovic. In the village of Grabovi, it was Zoran Kupreskic. In the village of Zume in Santici, it was Nenad Santic. Slavko Milicevic was in my village where I was. It was called Krcevine. He was a higher-level commander, and he often went to Vitez. He was always on the go. He drove a green van.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there, were these men known to you before the April '93 attack?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I knew them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were any of them distinguishable, one from the other, by the strength or extremity of their political views?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my opinion, Papic, who was in Zume, he was somewhat milder, so it seems that he saved some women and children from Zume. So in my opinion, he was less extreme.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't want your opinion, not because I don't want it but because it may be that it's not appropriate for your opinion to be given. But if you carry on with the answers, you've dealt with his being less of an extremist or more moderate and the women and children in that locality being saved. As to the other localities, with what strength or weakness did the commanders you've spoken of hold political views?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we're going to be assisted by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So be it. It's probably as far as I want to go, effective in any event. Yes, thank you very much. Wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm not sure if the matter that I raise has evidential significance, but it certainly has a human interest element that I find irresistible. Yesterday, the witness gave evidence that on the 16th of April, when the soldiers approached his house, he heard and recognised the voice of one of his Croatian neighbours. I think it's Ivo Papic. That neighbour effectively spurred the soldiers on to the Ahmic house, his house. I just want to find out what kind of relationship he had with this neighbour prior to this event.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, up to, we might say, 1992, our relations were good. After the tension, our relations as neighbours deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That deterioration, was it particular to you and this particular neighbour or was it similar to the deterioration in relationships that you may have encountered with other Croatians living in your village, Croats living in your village?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The overall relations changed, but we might say mostly on the side of the Croats, because they became aloof. They had their own goals, and we concluded this. They would turn away from us more and more. They most probably had certain aims they wanted to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apart from the general development of tension between the two communities, was there anything specific that brought about a decline in the relations between yourself and Ivo Papic?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, there was nothing specific, but mostly our relations cooled rapidly, not just between us but among the entire population of Ahmici and further afield.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope that clarifies the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, I don't have to tell you this, but nonetheless I should say publicly that we expect witnesses who have had experiences of this sort to be examined courteously and with restraint and expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: With respect, I hardly need to be reminded. What is the Court's pleasure relative to timing this morning, so I can gauge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Maybe we will take the break towards half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, Sir. Thank you. Sir, my name is Bob Stein. I represent Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My first question is do you speak or read the English language?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Very little. I don't speak and I don't read, but I learned some English at school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not getting the answer through my headset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can the answer be repeated, please?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't speak or read the English language, but I know a little, very little, because I learned English in secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir. If there's any question that I ask you that you don't understand, please let me know and I will repeat the question. Yesterday you testified that before the elections, relations between you and your neighbours were "relatively good". My question is this: What did you mean by "relatively good"?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I said "relatively good", I meant that we did not have extremely good relations. That's why I used the word "relatively".

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Is that to say that part of your relations were not good?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It depends. It varied from case to case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Would you give me some examples, please, of relationships that from case to case varied, showing the relationships were not good?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I will only tell you a general example. The Bosnian Croats essentially had a kind of behaviour. They didn't want to have extremely good relations. They were quite closed. They associated more among themselves, as far as I can tell. That's why I said "relatively".

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Do I take it that as a young boy and even into your teenage years, you were educated in schools under the Communist system that was the political authority in Bosnia during that time period?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I went to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As I understand it, the doctrines taught in those schools and held by the Communist Party were such that all peoples in Bosnia were to be brothers and treated equally.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: To the extent that if anyone deviated from that behaviour, that was condemned by the political system?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not really. Not completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Would you give me an example of how persons who spoke out against this system of Communism and brotherhood would be treated?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. They were condemned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Condemned by whom, sir?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: By the Communist government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. So the government held out as one of its views that everyone should be equal, treated equally, and those that didn't follow that doctrine were condemned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And therefore whatever was in the persons' actual hearts and minds and feelings was told to keep it quiet because the Communist system required a level of brotherhood; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Why did you resign from the SDA party before the war?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were no special reasons. But parties can change, and I preferred the SDP party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us why, please?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I say that a person can change political parties. He can leave one party to join another because the other party has a better programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What, specifically, attracted you to the other party's programme? This is my last question on this particular point.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't join the SDP but I left the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir. Now, do I take it that joining the TO was not compulsory?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: When you joined, did you join voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And do I take it further that when the HVO was formed, Muslims were allowed to join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed, the HVO asked Muslims to join them; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they didn't ask, but before the conflict of the 16th of April, 1993, they issued an ultimatum that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Central Bosnia should subordinate itself to the command of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm confusing you with my question. Let me orient you towards April of 1992. Can we agree that at that point in time, the HVO actually asked the Muslims to join it?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me orient the Prosecutor and yourself -- and I'll try to do it very quickly -- to your statement dated February 1, '97, at page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Nice and I can agree without the usual litany, quote: "The Muslims were allowed to join the TO at the time. HVO asked the Muslims to join their army, but the Muslims didn't do that." Can we agree that that's what the statement says, Mr. Nice? That's at the last paragraph; sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can agree that -- in the English version, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The English version says exactly what I've just said, sir. Would you now reconsider your answer to the question whether the HVO asked the Muslims to join them?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This could have been the case in the contacts between people who knew each other, and those who were called or invited by that way, they may have joined it in this way. But I doubt that this was placed in the media publicly. So it was just on a private basis among the people who knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir. And further, would you agree that amongst your people, amongst the local opinion, was that it was not right for the majority to join the minority? Again, this is taken directly from your statement, same date, page 2, last line.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, do I take it, sir, also, that generally, in October of 1992, there were 20 HVO soldiers living in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: They were guarding the village every night?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: They were guarding the village to protect from any Chetnik attacks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That was only provisionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good. And further, do I understand correctly that before your brother became commander of the local TO unit, Fuad Berbic -- that's F-U-A-D B-E-R-B-I-C -- had been the commander?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Fuad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fuad, yes. I apologise. Correct. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And there were, under his command as well as your brother's command, about 120 men in the defence of your village?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Some of the individuals had self-made camouflage outfits?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And others of the members, of the 120 members, had no uniforms at all?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And about one-third of this group were armed?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So if I understand it, the picture created is we have some individuals with camouflage and some without; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Some individuals with weapons and some without?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Therefore, do I take it, then, when they were on patrol, some of the individuals had weapons and camouflage?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Some did -- I'm sorry, some of the individuals would have weapons but no camouflage?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Some of the individuals would have neither a weapon nor camouflage?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that could also have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And some of the individuals would merely have camouflage and no weapon?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It depended. It was a case-by-case thing. It's not really crucial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Certainly. Yet nonetheless, weaponed, camouflaged, all or some of the individuals were on patrol, on guard in the village, as part of their duties?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Since the Croats had guards as well, we also kept our guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good. And the situation that I just described existed both in 1992 and in 1993 April?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, you could say that until the attack of 20 October '92. This was because we had to abolish these patrols in the lower part of the village because of this order by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: With respect to your answer, sir -- and I turn the Prosecution again to the February 1, 1997, statement, this time at page 5, the end of paragraph 24. Your statement of that date, at paragraph 24, reads, quote: "In 1993 there was still a village guard in the village of Ahmici. It functioned in the same way as in 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, have I got that correctly? Page 5, statement of February 1, '97.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Having read your statement into the record, sir, would you now like to reconsider your answer?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The guards in the upper part of the village functioned normally, as before; but in the lower part, people did go out on guard duties, but they did so stealthily. They would sort of hide their weapons, or something, so that in the case of some unforeseen attack, they would be able to inform the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Stein, in order for us to better understand what is being said, can you ask the witness whether there was a difference within these patrols at that time, in 1993, a distinction then between Upper Ahmici and Lower Ahmici? Because it seems that there is such a difference, so why is there such a difference? Because of the population living in Upper Ahmici and Lower Ahmici, or is this due to security reasons, different from the point of view of Upper Ahmici or Lower Ahmici? What's the difference? We have to establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you've heard the question of the Judge. Would you please describe whether there were two situations, Lower and Upper, and if so, the difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The command was a single one, but the circumstances were different, because the lower part of the village was under the HVO command, and they monitored our movements and whether we carried weapons, whereas the HVO did not have any of their command in the upper part of the village, so we could carry out normal patrols up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So to finish your answer, I believe the answer we just heard is that in the lower part of the village, the HVO did the patrols, whereas in the upper part, the TO did the patrols; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The HVO had very strong patrols in the lower part of the village, and they were monitoring our movements, especially if we carried -- whether we carried arms, because that was prohibited. As I said before, the guards would only show up surreptitiously, and only along the road, and people may have only carried pistols if they went out to patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: It's fair to say, is it not, that you also were monitoring the HVO activities? "You" meaning the TO.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot say so, because I was not a commander or a part of the staff. I can only speak about myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, with respect, sir, you certainly talked to your brother about TO activities, and other members of the TO, so I ask you the question again: Is it fair to say, based on not just what you did and saw yourself, but based on the common knowledge of what was going on in the TO, is it fair to say that you too, you also, were monitoring the activities of the HVO like they were monitoring you?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my statements, I said that we separately monitored the HVO activities following the conflict of 20 October, 1992. The HVO activities increased significantly after that, and my brother Muris at that time was part of no command of the Territorial Defence or later of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir. And that monitoring that you did after October of 1992 resulted in reports to the higher authorities; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Infrequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Those higher authorities would be where, sir?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The commands were in Vitez, Kruscica, and Preocica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir. There came a time -- oh, I'm sorry, let me back off one moment and ask you this question: From your description of the TO, it basically was a town guard, not a group of professional soldiers; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Nonetheless, in October of 1992, October 19th or 20th, your local organisation of town guards received an order to make a barricade and to block the road; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: From where did the order come?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From the Territorial Defence headquarters in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your statement of 3 February, '95, that's exactly what you said. However, I'm curious, because in your statement of 25 October, '94, page 2 -- and I'll wait for Mr. Nice to catch up. Middle of the page, or maybe two-thirds down, you set out, quote: "We had received orders from Sarajevo to prevent such large forces from going to Travnik, so we put up a roadblock in the village of Ahmici." Do you recall, sir, whether the order came from Vitez or from Sarajevo or from some other location?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: According to the chain of command, the main headquarters was in Sarajevo, and I assume that probably they called Vitez from Sarajevo and ordered them something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. And who would be the person in that chain of command who gave the order?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean at the top level?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that it was Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And below him, would there be someone else who potentially could have given the order?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Vitez, there was -- I believe that Hakija Cengic was commander of the Territorial Defence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me ask you clearly: Do you know specifically who did give this particular order?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know specifically, but I know that it came from the headquarters in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good. There is a group called the Coordinating Committee for Protection of Muslims, is there not?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. And another question along the same lines: Would it have been possible for General Merdan, of the 7th Corps, to have given this particular order -- 3rd Corps, sorry.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, there were no corps. There were only Territorial Defence staffs. At that time, the corps had not yet been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. Regardless of whether the corps had been established or not, would it have been possible for Dzemal Merdan to have issued this order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness says that the corps hadn't been established, so what he is saying is that the order couldn't have come from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I think there is a gap in the logic there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's not assisting us. Let's move on. It would be pure supposition on his part. His evidence is that the order came from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, in preparation to blockade the road, among the various things you did was gather mines, landmines; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And mines had been taken from a warehouse before October 20?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were no warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Where were the mines kept before the action of October 20?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know where they were, but as far as I know, those mines were brought from the Slimena depot near Travnik. When it was blown up, then those mines were brought down there. I don't know by whom, and I don't know who kept them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Right. As I understand it, the JNA basically left those mines behind. Your troops took the mines into the various homes and held them until they were necessary to be used; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: With respect to this warehouse, the JNA had blown it up, and then it was just a free-for-all as to who would get what, and I believe that the Croats got much more than we did. I think that they even put up different checkpoints where they would wait for the Muslims to pass through, and then they would collect it from them on the way back to Vitez. So as far as weapons are concerned, the Croats managed to get more weapons from that warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: With respect, sir, let me try to make myself clear. Whatever weapons you did have were kept at individual homes as opposed to one central location? This is relative to the mines, and generally, weapons.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, other preparations that you made before the October 20 barricade were to dig trenches; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Very few trenches were dug, only around the barricade, in order to protect the men who were manning the barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And on one side of the barricade was a Catholic cemetery; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You dug trenches in that Catholic cemetery; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that is not correct, because Croats were coming during the daylight to check on it, and it was impossible to dig trenches there. The trenches were dug on the opposite side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did you use any part of the Catholic cemetery for protection and as part of this barricade?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know, because I was not at the barricade. I only know that no trenches were dug in the Catholic cemetery. That was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this: The men at the barricade from your village were joined by other villagers to help man the barricade; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only the people from our village were there, there were no others, but other people came for protection -- that is, from other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe I'm confused. Other people did come from other villages for -- "protection"? Is that the word you used?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. People came from the village of Vrhovine, as minor assistance, for the most part to just protect the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Were they at the barricade itself, sir, from your understanding?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they were not. As far as I know, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And there were about 200 other people who came from other villages to help protect yours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not say 200. Up to 100 came from outside to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir. I'll accept that. These individuals who came to help you, also, some of them had camouflage?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And some of them were armed?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, continuing along the same lines, let me take a look, please, at exhibit -- this is in the bundle 1593B; it's specifically 21479A. It's the photo of the minaret.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you, and can the witness have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, let me first ask you, there appears to be another small minaret in the picture on the lower left-hand side. Where would that minaret be in your village?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The lower minaret was on this mosque, but it was constructed earlier. It was the entryway to the mosque. I think that there was an additional one, but it cannot be seen here. It was not another mosque. It is just part of the same mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. The minaret that is in the foreground, the very tall structure, on the top part, coming out right here (indicating) -- take a look at where I'm pointing. I'm afraid I can't go over there -- appear to be some sort of microphones or loudspeakers. Is that what they are?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I take it from these loudspeakers -- do I take it from these loudspeakers your fellow Muslims were called to prayer?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And was this minaret with its loudspeakers also used to make announcements or tell villagers of problems or Chetniks or any other type thing?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Were any orders ever called out from the minaret?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have not heard about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Was the loudspeaker and the minaret at the mosque in Ahmici used to call upon the Croatian people to hand over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Relative to anything you may have heard, as opposed to what you, yourself, have heard with your own ears, did you ever hear anyone in the village talk about the minaret and the loudspeakers being used for that particular purpose?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I have not heard about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do I take it, sir, that there were steps leading up to the top of the minaret of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: When you got to the top, how far could you see from the minaret?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never climbed up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do you know, from people who did, what kind of vantage point or view they would have?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Probably a good view, because it was a pretty high minaret, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, it's now half past eleven Is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll take the break for 20 minutes. I very much hope that this examination can be concluded in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, in order to finish the cross-examination today of both you and Mr. Kovacic, we will extend the sitting until half past one in order to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: If necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna adds, "If necessary," of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, again let me focus on the exhibit and on the mosque. To your knowledge, at any time in October of 1992 or thereafter, leading up to April of 1993, did anybody with a weapon of any sort climb to the top of this particular minaret?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, at your home, did you keep ammunition for rifles?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Certainly other individuals of the TO had ammunition at their home; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Presumably, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: There was no central storage location for ammunition; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There wasn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly how much ammunition was allotted to individuals in the TO for storage at their home?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, nobody restricted the quantity. They had only as much ammunition as they could get, but they had very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, according to your testimony yesterday, there were 60 armed men at the barricade, and that's specifically referenced at the original Livenotes at 96:4. Do you know, first from your own personal views or what you heard, how many rounds of ammunition each one of those 60 armed men had?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know they had very little, because had they had more ammunition, they would have kept the barricade, the roadblock, because since they ran short of ammunition, they had to give up both the barricade and part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I understood, and that was your testimony yesterday. But my question is, sir, do you know, from any information you received, how many rounds each individual man carried or collectively there were available for the men on the barricades?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Judging by those people who had weapons there, they couldn't have had more than two, and most, I would guess, only one round, one magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. How many bullets in each magazine?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there were supposed to be 30 bullets per magazine, but of course it depended on how many he had and how many he charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Assuming that each individual had at least two rounds or 60 bullets and there were 60 armed men who used all of those rounds of ammunition, that's roughly 3.600 bullets being used in the defence of this barricade; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it is not because you say they had two magazines each, but very few of them had two magazines. The question is whether they were fully loaded or not. It is very difficult to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Certainly. I understand that. But we can agree that regardless of the number of magazines, regardless of the number of rounds, there were sufficient rounds of ammunition to hold the barricade from the early morning hours of October 20th until mid-afternoon; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, true. I mean just barely enough to hold it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do you have information as to how many members of the HVO were either wounded or killed during this assault on the barricade?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard that a fellow from Kiseljak was killed. I don't know how many were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As I understand, after the barricade was abandoned there were two to three houses in your village that were burned and roughly 20 stables. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that two or three houses had been burned and that 10 or 15 stables burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let me turn your attention, please, to the map which we've already seen, and I'll be done with the barricade. Specifically, may the witness have before him Z1585/1? There are two versions, both of which have been marked. It's this one that I'm looking at. Let's just double-check that we're talking about the same thing. For the purpose of the record, and maybe the Registrar can help us, we have two Z1585/1 that look identical. May it please the Court, and I don't want to make any confusion about this, the number I've just used, which is what we have here, actually has markings on it, so I assume there's a second version of this. Well, there's no markings on what the usher has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, there is one marked plan, because the witness marked a plan yesterday. That's the one you want him to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right, very good. May I see it? We'll work with this one. Would you put it on the ELMO, please, and specifically the area of section 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's where the roadblock was situated; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Would you take a green pen which is before you now, green magic marker, and would you show us on Z1585/1 where the trenches were by actually drawing a line in green to show the trench?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Witness complies)

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Would you bear down on that so we can have it, please, I mean really mark it hard? I can barely see it.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Witness complies)

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Would you put a "T" on top of that, just the letter "T"?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Witness complies)

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Would you show us again, in green, where the barricade was? Was that number 5?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Strike that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Was there also a stone wall that was used to protect the TO people?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know of any stone wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The cemetery is the white area below the "5", is it not?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: There's a wall blocking the road and -- I'm sorry. There's a wall between the road and the cemetery, is there not, a stone-type wall?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it wasn't a wall, it was a fence, and you could see through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. Would you put where that fence is, please, with again green?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Witness complies) The whole cemetery was surrounded by that fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Would you just mark, to the left-hand side, the letter "F" for "Fence"?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Witness complies)

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's all we have for that exhibit. Now I would like to turn our attention, please, to April 15, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do I take it, going back to this exhibit we marked, do you want to give that another identification number? Feel free.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: April 15, 1993, you testified yesterday that the evening was very quiet, absolutely alarmingly quiet, as I understand your testimony. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that several days, not only that evening only. I said that three or four days prior to the attack were quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You personally became concerned; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It was your testimony that nonetheless your concern was not shared by the rest of the community?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me, if I may, ask you -- excuse me, let me strike that. Would you please have available Defence 13/2, specifically, and this is the statement of Faud Berbic? I'm specifically, Mr. Nice, pointing to the address --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, don't address counsel across the Chamber. It's not courteous. You will address the Bench, and if you want counsel to do something, you can do it through the Bench. It's the normal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm specifically pointing to page 5, the fourth full paragraph, and again I think we established this before, but Mr. Berbic was the prior commander of the TO, yes, before your brother?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And he had substantial military experience, did he not?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's what you think. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He was a captain in the JNA, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard, but a reserve one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. In any event, according to that particular statement which is marked in evidence, and I quote for you: "On the eve of 15 April" -- I'm sorry. "On the eve of the 15 April attack, I was on guard duty. It was very quiet, dead calm. Our level of alertness had been increased by 50 per cent compared to the night before because unfamiliar uniformed persons had been seen. Ten men were on standby in the lower part of the village in addition to the guards, and the guards were doubled in the upper part of the village as well." My question to you, sir, is: Is it fair to say that on the evening of the 15th, there was an increased level of alertness?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was, according to what Fuad Berbic stated. But had there been a higher degree of alertness, not so many people would have been at home and therefore killed in the morning, slain in the morning. So this is Fuad Berbic's statement, and Fuad Berbic was not the commander at that time. It was Midhat Berbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I take it you personally were not on the barricade, or either -- let me strike that. That's confusing. You were not on patrol on April 15th, yourself?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, I was at home. I had no duty to discharge that night, nor my brother Muris, nor many others of us who were in their houses that night and were therefore slain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Therefore, of your own personal knowledge, you don't know whether Mr. Berbic's observations of a heightened alert and an increase of 50 per cent are accurate or not; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, true, I have no knowledge of that. It is his statement, and I really feel reluctant to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good. I just want to touch on this very briefly: There came a point in time on the 16th of April where you, yourself, surrendered a grenade to the HVO forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your brother had also surrendered a grenade?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that. I did not see that, but I know he had a hand grenade and I had a hand grenade. That was all the weapons that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm just looking for one thing, Your Honour, in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers who were surrounding your home specifically said something to you along the lines that there had been a massacre at Dusina and at Nezirovici; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You were aware of those facts, when they happened or shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew very little about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You knew, however, that there had been Croats killed?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you knew also that the Muslims of the 7th Brigade had been the ones, supposedly, who had done that killing?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't know who was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Certainly you did know that it was claimed that Muslims killed Croats?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stein, I think we ought to know something about what your case is about Ahmici. The witness's evidence is that his house was attacked and his family killed. I take it that that is accepted? It hasn't been challenged?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It is accepted that his house was attacked and that his family was killed. Our position on the subject generally is that Mr. Kordic knew nothing about the attack on Ahmici, had nothing to do with its planning, was not there, and only learned about it after the fact. I will also tell the Court, having read the transcripts and the other testimony in the other cases, it's apparent from those cases, at least, that there is some dispute as to whether the village was prepared or not, whether the village was armed and defended or not, and whether or not the village was actually the subject of a military action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I presume it's not disputed that there was some military action there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it going to be suggested in this trial that there was a defence or that there wasn't an attack by the HVO on the village?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Oh, no, there was a conflagration. Who started it, who defended it, frankly, from our perspective, since we had nothing to do with it, is not largely relevant. That was my first answer to Your Honour's question. I want to be clear, our position is he had nothing to do with it. On the other hand, it would be an abrogation of duty on our parts to just let the record roll on without indicating that there are other sources of evidence which clearly indicate this was a two-sided affair. I'm not here to say who started, or who fired the first weapon, or the motives of the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The one piece of evidence which was given involving Mr. Kordic was the threat -- which, you'll remember, was the subject of objection -- that their houses would be burnt and the people would be killed, and it's alleged that this was said to be a message from Dario Kordic. Is it challenged that there was such a message?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely challenged there was such a message. I remember the colloquy well, and that was part of my response to Your Honour in arguing the motion. We never said that. Mr. Kordic never said that, nor was anyone authorised to say it in his name. Now, there may be some other evidence about it, and we'll challenge that, but our position is that the threat which has been introduced by the Prosecutor initially to have been Mr. Kordic's, and then the position changed somewhat to be in the name of Mr. Kordic, was neither his to give, nor did he give it, nor was it authorised in his name. And further, the reason I brought out what I did was that although two to three homes and ten stables were burned, according to the witness, after the October attack, that was the limit of that attack. After the blockade was over, the troops moved through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Stein, you have just said that Mr. Kordic, the accused Kordic, was not aware before, was not aware of what had happened in Ahmici, but that he learned about it later on. This is exactly what you said, isn't it? I noted that properly? Could you tell us when he learned about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I frankly don't have that information off the tip of my head; that is, the day -- the next day or shortly thereafter. I will get that for you and report back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You are very cooperative today. Today is Friday, the last day of the week. Let's use that--

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I like to think I'm cooperative every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Let's avail ourselves of this opportunity, because you are extremely kind and willing to cooperate. So you're going to tell us when he knew about it and whether he took steps, you know, he did anything accordingly? When did he hear about it, and when he did, when he heard about all these facts we have just heard, did he take any steps accordingly? We would be very grateful for that in order to establish the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, you said your case was that this was a two-sided affair. Of course, of importance in that is whether a particular side was acting defensively and another aggressively. I imagine you're saying that there is no onus on you to show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You create a doubt about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
