utterances.text: What I'm trying to say, clearly, and not to duck Your Honour's question, is I don't know, nor does Mr. Kordic, who were the aggressors and who were the defenders, and at any given time. The attack went on for hours. Who fired first, we don't know. How -- the manner of defence, who got the better of it, we don't know, nor is it important for our case, except to say that there were, according to other trials in this Tribunal, there's a lot of evidence all along those lines. I hope not to have a trial within a trial on a defence to an action that we didn't have anything to do with, but I wanted at least -- and I think it was our duty to show that there are two sides to this particular story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stein. Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I hope you, too, can conclude within the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, rest assured, I will finish it in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ahmic. I'm Goran Mikulicic, a lawyer, a member of the Defence team representing Mr. Mario Cerkez in this case. Before I ask you some questions, I should like to ask you to believe me when I say that I truly sympathise with you, that I do understand your loss, and I really feel sorry about all that you suffered during the case in Ahmici and the whole conflict in Bosnia. Now, Mr. Ahmic, could you please tell us, what nationality, what citizenship did you hold until April 1992, and that is until the day when the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed its sovereignty and independence?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yugoslav citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you were a national of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; is it so?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us, which nationality, which citizenship did you hold after Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed its independence? That is, after April '92.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The citizenship of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Ahmic, are you a practising believer?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time, I mean 1992 and 1993, did you perform any religious rituals in the mosque in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, could you tell us, to the best of your recollection, how many men of your age, at the time, regularly go to mosque for the purpose of religious service?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could give you a percentage. It could be some 50 or maybe 60 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, in your statement, you testified that on the eve of the events on the 20th of October, '92, you said that your brother Muris commanded the TO in the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you then tell us, how long was he the commander of the TO?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think until the 23rd of October '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you please correct me if I'm wrong. I believe you said that he resigned after that; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, or he was dismissed. I'm not quite clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know the reasons for his resignation, i.e., dismissal?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, not quite, not really, but roughly he was quite disappointed with what was going on, and he thought it was his mistake, that he was responsible for all the damage. I believe he was very disappointed with what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who succeeded him?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Midhat Berbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A while ago you said that Midhat Berbic also held that position in April 1993; that is, at the time of the second conflict, if I may call it that, in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, is Midhat the son of Fuad Berbic?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We talked about this roadblock in October '92 that had been erected on the road going through Ahmici. Could you tell us, what kind of a road is that?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it is a regional road, one could say. It's not a highway. It linked various regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, which regions did that particular road link?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, East Bosnia and West Bosnia. East with West Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the road we're referring to, now looking westward, comes from Travnik, and then one can follow it to Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, tell us, do you know -- and we are talking about the latter half of October '92 -- was there any fighting around Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who participated in that fighting?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the BH army on one hand and the HVO, on one side, against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So is it true that the BH army, together with the HVO, resisted the Serb attack in Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, Judge Robinson asked you today something about Ivo Papic. Just to clarify matters further, tell us, was Mr. Ivo Papic one of those who helped you escape from the house in which you were at the time when you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I shall now ask you, Mr. Ahmic, to answer the following questions with "Yes" or "No" only, to try to go through them quickly. Is it true that you told us that you were hiding in that ditch next to the road after you had managed to escape from the Upper, that is, Central Ahmici, and you watched soldiers passing by the road?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not flee Central Ahmici. I fled from my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, right. But is it true that at the time you happened to see the insignia they wore on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you told us that after, when you were so cold and wet in the ditch, having spent there all night, you got to the cinders of a house, which was still smouldering, to get warm?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you told us that from that house, you could hear from a nearby house the voice of your mother?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you heard her sob and cry how her husband and children had been killed?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you said there was fog and you couldn't see much?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, this is the end of my examination. You mentioned that you were taken to the elementary school in Dubravica, together with other Bosniaks, and I want to ask you something in this regard. Is it true that that facility was guarded by the special unit Vitezovi Knights, as you claimed in your earlier statements given to Court investigators?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, do you know who commanded that special unit?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The camp commander was Anto Krisanac, a man on the short side, rather dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But who was the commander of Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it was Kraljevic, the one that was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Ahmic. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a few points.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about the number of weapons held by the Territorial Defence in Ahmici. But leading up to April 1993, what sort of level of arms was held within the village? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Up to April 1993, there were not many weapons because the people who had gone from the Territorial Defence and entered the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where battalions were set up, were now in a different situation. They had to go to the nearby war theatres against the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Vlasic or in Visoko, so that we were much weaker in the period up to April 1992 as regards weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The translation came as "1992", but did you mean up to 1993?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I think there were fewer and fewer weapons because the people and the weapons they had, they had to take the weapons to the front lines, and the weapons were left on the defence lines facing the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate at all how many armed men there were in Ahmici on a day or on a night in March or April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Nobody carried weapons in the daytime. And at night, people would come out to patrol, and it's hard to estimate, but I often saw them patrolling and they were not big patrols. It was mostly old-age pensioners who patrolled, because most of the young people were outside Ahmici at the positions. And sometimes there would be shifts, and when the attack broke out, then the younger people who were killed happened to be at home but they didn't have their weapons with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The men, you say mostly old-age pensioners who did patrol, what level of arms and ammunition did they have, typically?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We might say 10 to 20 barrels or pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just so I understand that, by "barrels", do you mean something like a rifle, and do you mean 10 to 20 altogether?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Altogether, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the time leading up to the middle of April of 1993, was there any plan, of which you were aware, to attack the HVO in your locality or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, (interpretation) I object to this question. It seems to me that my colleague is going outside the area covered in the examination in chief and the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you answer the question? Was there any plan of which you were aware to attack the HVO in your locality or anywhere else in the period leading up to the middle of April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of any such plan, but that would not be very probable because we had big problems at the lines facing the Serbs to keep the little territory we held, so it was absolutely impossible for us. But the attacks against the HVO had to be carried out, such as they were, because the Croats started incidents and we had to respond. But this was an absolute necessity, because if we had had any plans to attack the HVO, it would have been self-destruction on our part because we couldn't fight two enemies at once. I mean we couldn't start a conflict with two enemies at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In that period up until April 1993, what, if any, access did the Territorial Defence have to weapons so that it could, if at all, increase its level of arms?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In that period, the army was established. There may have been some channels for the supply of weapons, but I think very few weapons arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did any weapons come from those channels to Ahmici, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no. We had only the weapons that we managed to bring from Slimena, and some people may have bought rifles on the black market just before the war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the morning itself of the 16th of April, when you were woken up, from your house did you have any view from your house of other parts of Ahmici on the other side of the road?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you either able to see -- or even if able, did you have the time to focus on what was happening on the other side of the road?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had very little time, and I was looking out of the window to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see any signs of attack being mounted by residents of Ahmici or by the Territorial Defence against others?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice that. I was not able to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: During the day that you spent in the stream or ditch, did you see any signs of attack by residents of Ahmici or the Territorial Defence on others?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I was unable to see that, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, you've been asked, in respect of an earlier incident, about the details of the roadblock by the cemetery and about, for example, the use of mines. How did this roadblock compare, if at all, with roadblocks erected by the HVO? Was it similar, stronger, weaker, better armed, worse armed?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The HVO roadblocks had a lot of hedgehogs, a lot of mines, with soldiers armed to the teeth with machine gun nests, with support. But all we had were mines and two iron hedgehogs which were set up, and the people manned the checkpoint to stop the traffic, and they dug a few trenches at the side of the road, which I marked, and that is what the roadblock was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I wish to ask the witness in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Judge, I'm not sure the Court knows, and I don't, what an iron hedgehog is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, would you tell us what a hedgehog is, please?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is two iron pieces of rail tracks, iron tracks. They are very heavy, and they are placed in the shape of a cross and put on the road to prevent vehicles from passing through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ahmici. That concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the International Tribunal to give evidence. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in a position to start another witness straightaway. I recognise that he won't be obviously completed today, but unless the Court thinks otherwise, we have half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we can use the time until 1.15, which was the original time we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are summaries that may be distributed. I'm sorry they haven't been distributed earlier, but they've only recently been concluded. Defence have got them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope the usher is bringing the witness in, but he may not have known what was expected of him. While --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the area that this witness deals with, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is Vitez, but it's particular matters. Here he comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Munib Kajmovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, were you born in Kadice, some 16 kilometres from Vitez, and were you, from 1976 and until April of 1993, a history teacher at the Vitez high school?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Just a small correction. I was not born in Kadice but in Kundici, in the municipality of Travnik. But it's true I have been employed as a history teacher in the high school in Vitez from 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As it happened, did you encounter Dario Kordic as a pupil at your school for a year or so?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What age was he when he was at the Vitez high school?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Since I started teaching at the Vitez high school in 1976, then I taught a third grade class, and Dario Kordic was a pupil in that class.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You'll have to help us with the age of somebody in the third grade, please, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, pupils graduate from high school, which lasts four years, at the age of 18, more or less. So he might have been 16 or 17 years old at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that stage, was there one characteristic of him that you noted as being a little unusual?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: While that is a detail, since someone who works in a school sees a lot of generations passing through and then you remember some pupils by some details and don't remember others, but Dario Kordic sticks in my memory because several times he stopped me in the corridor and asked me additional questions in history which mostly referred to the history of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that time, was history taught in a way that focused or encouraged the focus on national history of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The curriculum was such that national history was taught but so was general history. In national history, topics which might have an effect on national relations were avoided because Yugoslavia was a state composed of various ethnic groups, and that is what the system demanded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, regarding the teaching of history, could we know from the witness whether that curriculum taught at Vitez was a curriculum established at national level?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Does that mean that the same curriculum was taught everywhere in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly, yes. But in particular republics, a certain percentage of the curriculum was allowed to be devoted to national history according to the amount of time given to it. For example, in Slovenia, the pupils learned a little more about Slovenian national history, the history of the Slovenes, but as a rule there were no major differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the absence of objection, I will be able to deal with the balance of the paragraphs on page 1 and halfway down page 2 by "Yes"/"No" questions and answers or by summary. If my friends opposite want anything to be dealt with extensively, no doubt they will indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, I think you'll be able to answer these questions "Yes" or "No" without elaboration, for the most part, in order to save time, because we are covering matters that have been covered or can be covered elsewhere. Is it right that you joined the SDA party in 1990 and became its president in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to deal with it but leaping to the time after the conflict, did you, in 1994, become a graduate student in politics at the university in Sarajevo, completing a thesis on political and demographic changes in the Vitez municipality, and although your thesis has been completed, it has yet to be defended before the faculty in accordance with the system that operates there?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my thesis has been completed. I have two or three issues left to deal with, and then I will defend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You would be able, if asked, to deal with the development of tension between the HDZ and the SDA in the build-up to the conflict. Just one detail. How did the HDZ attempt to persuade people to join it, if at all?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Since up to 1990, in Yugoslavia, there was a one-party system, in 1990, when the laws permitted the introduction of a multi-party system, several political parties were established, and some of them were established on a national basis, even though not all of them were established on that basis. In this period, every party tried to attract as many sympathisers and members as possible, so that all the parties did that, and most of the parties tried to do so by criticising the ruling party, by advocating their own party programme, and a lot of work was done in the field to convince people that they should support such and such a political party, that these were times which would probably see major changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I stop you there and take you from that general description of the development of multi-party politics to the narrower issue? Are those the methods that the HDZ used or did they on occasions use different methods, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, no force was used, but gradually at the local level in Vitez, I noticed that the leading structures of the HDZ adopted a rather negative attitude toward those Croats who did not easily accept their programme. Especially they had a negative attitude toward those people who remained members of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia and the SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are there any particular methods of recruitment associated with the HDZ that stick in your memory and that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I can mention an example of two Croats from Vitez. One of them was Stipo Brka, who is still employed at the municipal assembly at Vitez. I think he's in the land registry, and he was a member of the Communist Party, the SDP. The other one was Zdravko Livancic. They remained loyal to the Communist Party of Yugoslavia or the Party of Democratic Changes. Then the HDZ, at a certain moment with the help of soldiers, burst into the building of the then open university where the offices of the Communist Party and all the other parties were located, and they smashed up the office. In their offices, these two Croats happened to be there at the time, and they tied them up and then they put them in a vehicle and took them to a place called Zabrdze in the area of Vitez, where they tied them to a tree, beat them up, fired shots from firearms. They didn't kill them. But when they got back, I had the opportunity of meeting Stipo Brka, who was too scared to talk about this event. He mostly kept silent, and I can say that he remained very consistent, that he persisted in his political convictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, Mr. Kajmovic. I think we might move on now to other topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you assume that Vitez had become part of Herceg-Bosna without ever seeing any official publication to that effect until after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I assumed that something like this was possible, even though later on, by following these issues, I understood that the HDZ structures on 18 November, 1991, had actually proclaimed this Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to cut you short, because some of these questions can be dealt with just by "Yes" or "No" answers. In particular, I think you became a member of the crisis committee in April 1992, in Vitez, and Ivica Santic was president of that committee?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At one of the crisis meetings, Anto Valenta said something that you can recall; just tell us, please, what it was he said, in summary, in respect of the behaviour of Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the crisis staff, there were often discussions on various issues, and the Bosniak and Croat members of the crisis staff often disagreed on the solutions to certain problems, and whenever there would be an issue where we could not agree -- and at one point Anto Valenta was quite upset and said something like, "Watch out, you Bosniaks, what you are doing and how you are debating the crisis staff, because we are armed by 90 per cent, and as far as we know, you are only armed by 10 per cent, and so you may pay a very steep price for what you are doing." So that was sort of the gist of his statement at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can, if asked, deal with the development of aggression from Serbia and Montenegro, with the SDA offering a joint Defence force, with Anto Valenta becoming president of the HDZ, and with Anto Valenta requesting a meeting of elected deputies of the municipal assemblies at an elementary school in Vitez where he invited recognition of Herceg-Bosna and where the Muslim representatives refused. I set those things out. You can, if asked by other people, deal with them in detail? Just "Yes" or "No," please.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1992, the HVO was created, and it took over municipal authorities in the police stations. And you can help, if asked, with the developing pattern of Croats wearing uniforms with HVO badges, with the dismissal of Bosniaks from the police, with the request of Bosnian Muslims to sign loyalty agreements, and with the fact that those who declined to sign lost their jobs? Again, if asked, you can deal with all those things in detail?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, you were, yourself, present at a meeting in Novi Travnik where Dario Kordic, in military uniform, dealt with the demand for two multi-rocket launchers from the Bratstvo factory? Again, just "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think at this point, since the accused entered into the picture, it might be helpful to have this matter dealt with, if the Trial Chamber deems it to be non-cumulative and relevant, by non-leading questions, and I would point out that we have already had witnesses who have testified about this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it should be dealt with conventionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm happy to deal with it conventionally, of course, or alternatively, because it's been dealt with already by other witnesses and I'm not sure that its been materially challenged, simply to be dealt with as a topic he can deal with if asked, to save time. I think perhaps the best course is for me to return to that after the weekend, when I've seen if there is anything truly challenged in the previous testimony that needs to be dealt with, and I can move on swiftly, for the purpose of this stage of the evidence, as the Court knows, is to avoid cumulative evidence. Paragraph 15, however, is, I think, new, and I'll deal with it conventionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Slimena factory close to Travnik, was there an incident there in May of 1992 that you can help us with?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is a warehouse, it's a weapons depot, not a factory. And indeed there was an incident there that took place -- I believe it was on 4 May, 1992, and I could explain what actually happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In summary, because we don't need it in the greatest detail, if you can, simply in your own words, in a few sentences, explain what happened and what the outcome was.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: This was a depot of the former JNA where, several months previously, it had transferred the weapons of the Territorial Defence of three municipalities, Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Vitez. They controlled it, and in May 1992, the HVO armed forces attacked this depot. The security of the JNA withdrew. Part of the depot was set on fire during the attack, and some of the equipment was burned, and then the population, in an organised and unorganised way, arrived from all three municipalities and took these weapons -- that is, from Novi Travnik, Travnik, and Vitez. I was there for about three -- I was there after -- this was just following a meeting, and I was there for about three hours -- about three hours later, after it had taken place, and I saw four to five thousand people taking weapons with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would it be possible to give any estimate as to the proportion of one ethnic group or another that was represented in this four to five thousand people?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: The attack on this military depot was carried out by the HVO. I don't know if there were any members of the army who took part in it, but our assessment was that the HVO wanted to take over these weapons, and we thought that no Bosniaks would receive any -- would get any of these weapons. We thought the HVO perhaps would not need those weapons as much, but that they wanted to prevent them from falling into the hands of the Bosniaks, either through negotiations or any other means. In support of this claim was the fact that that morning when the attack was carried out, the HDZ and SDA representatives from Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Vitez arrived and held a meeting in the municipal building in Travnik, and there we proposed that the weapons be distributed equally, so that 50 per cent would go to the Croatian side and 50 to the Bosniak side, and that this also be evenly distributed among the three municipalities, even though the municipalities did not have equal-size populations or equal amounts of armaments. But in field, they practically were not able to prevent the Bosniak population from taking some of the weapons, and even their own people, because it was a chaotic situation, and no order could be established. Even had we established any kind of -- reached any kind of agreement within the municipal building, we wouldn't have been able to implement it because of the chaotic situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, in the next question but one, whether today or next week, about an event in a Vitez stadium where you saw Dario Kordic at an oath-taking ceremony. Can you, for the present purposes, simply give an idea of what part of 1992 that occurred? Spring, summer, autumn, winter?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, they had a parade --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I just want the timing at the moment: Spring, summer, autumn, winter?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: It may have been the summer, end of the summer. At any rate, it was hot. I remember that one soldier got sick and needed to be given help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the time between your first getting involved in these political matters and this meeting or this event at the stadium in the summer of 1992, had you had any encounters with your sometime school pupil, Dario Kordic? Had you met him, spoken to him at all?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I did not meet him until there were some negotiations at the local level. The representatives of Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Novi Travnik would come, and then we held meetings. This was in late 1992; in fact, starting mid-1992. There were several such meetings, and in some of these meetings, Dario Kordic was also present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 22 -- and this may be a convenient place to end, subject to the Court's decisions on its timetable -- at these meetings, what views did he express? In general terms.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: In the meetings, several issues were discussed, and solutions were sought; that is, political solutions, starting with the local authorities, police, and then military, the symbols and insignia that should be used. In these discussions, his positions were fairly extreme. It was very difficult to look for a compromise that would be acceptable for both sides. I think that they were not leading towards solving problems but, rather, further friction among the ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have perhaps one minute of matters to inform the Court about, administrative matters, and this would be as convenient a moment as any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the witness could withdraw, and possibly just a private session for one minute, then I can inform the Court of the timetable for next week and the weeks after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, we are going to adjourn now. Would you be back, please, on Monday morning at 9.45? Would you remember -- no, there's one thing I want to tell you. Mr. Kajmovic, I'm sorry to detain you, but there's one thing I want to say, and I must say it in public: Please don't speak to anybody about your evidence over the weekend, and that includes members of the Prosecution. If you would like to go now, and be back on Monday morning, please.
